buffet

/BUFF-it/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Buffet means to strike something over and over with force.

For three days, storm waves buffeted the old wooden pier until several planks tore loose.

Example

High on the exposed ridge, gusts buffeted the hiker so hard that she had to crouch behind a boulder to catch her breath.

The wind doesn't hit the hiker once — it strikes her again and again with real force. That repetition plus force is the heart of buffet.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

pound: Pound means to hit something heavily again and again, stressing the weight behind each blow — fists pound a door, surf pounds the rocks. Buffet stresses the relentless repetition more than the heaviness: winds buffet a hiker, knocking her about blow after blow without any single crushing strike.

pummel: To pummel is to rain blows on someone or something, classically with fists, hard enough that the target comes away hurt. Buffet shares the repetition but not the damage: winds that buffet a bridge rattle and shake it, yet everything is still standing when they die down.

thrash: Thrash means to hit violently and repeatedly, often with the flailing motion of a whip or a beating handed out in anger. Buffet is blunter and more impersonal — the steady slamming of wind, waves, or events against whatever stands in their way, with no fury behind it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

caress: to touch gently and softly

cushion: to soften a blow or impact

Where it sits · how hard the blows land

jostle → buffet → batter

jostle vs. buffet: To jostle is to bump or push lightly; to buffet is to strike again and again with real force.

batter vs. buffet: Batter is stronger than buffet — if winds buffet a fence they rattle and shake it, but if they batter it, they leave it broken.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — buffe: a blow, a slap (Old French, probably imitating the sound of a hit landing)

Suffix — -et: little; a diminutive ending

Put it together: Buffet began as Old French bufet, literally 'a little blow' — and to buffet something is to land blow after blow after blow on it.

Use the root in a new word: buffet (the meal): The all-you-can-eat buffet is a different word entirely — French for 'sideboard,' and no relation. Our buffet, 'to strike again and again,' came from Old French bufet, 'a little blow,' probably coined to imitate the sound of a slap, and it built no other common English words.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Neutral / slightly literary

Pronounced BUFF-it — this word is completely unrelated to the buh-FAY meal table, which just happens to share the spelling. It often appears in the passive ('the coast was buffeted by gales') and works figuratively too: a company can be buffeted by criticism or bad news.
